marrow__PHYS_CH11_Q011.takeaway: Heat nociceptors begin responding at about 45 °C, the source-keyed threshold among the options.
marrow__PHYS_CH11_Q011.displayText:
The source-keyed answer is approximately 45 °C for heat-pain fibers. The source table distinguishes ordinary temperature-receptor peaks from nociceptor activation thresholds: the cold-receptor peak is about 24 °C and the warm-receptor peak about 45 °C; cold nociceptors are stimulated around 5 °C, while heat nociceptors begin responding around 45 °C.

The source also lists cold-receptor afferents as Aδ and C fibers and warm-receptor afferents as unmyelinated C fibers. These are separate temperature-receptor categories; the question asks specifically for the heat-pain threshold.
emphasis: warm-receptor afferents as unmyelinated C fibers

Warm receptor fibers: unmyelinated C fibers

rationales.b: 49 °C is above the approximate onset; the keyed threshold is around 45 °C, not 49 °C.
rationales.d: 35 °C is below the approximate temperature at which heat-pain fibers begin responding.

marrow__PHYS_CH11_Q012.takeaway: The Weber–Fechner law relates perceived sensation magnitude to the logarithm of stimulus intensity.
marrow__PHYS_CH11_Q012.displayText:
The Weber–Fechner law relates the magnitude of a perceived sensation to the logarithm of stimulus intensity, so the source-keyed choice is “Log of intensity of stimulus.”

The source also distinguishes two other sensory principles. The doctrine of specific nerve energies says that activating a sensory pathway produces the modality for which that pathway is specialized, regardless of where along it the activation begins. The law of projection says that stimulation anywhere along a sensory pathway is perceived as arising from the pathway's receptor location.

rationales.a: Muscle-contraction strength is not the variable in the Weber–Fechner relationship.
rationales.c: Action-potential amplitude is largely all-or-none; stimulus intensity is reflected by firing frequency and recruitment, not spike amplitude.
rationales.d: Stimulus duration is not the quantity related to sensation magnitude by the Weber–Fechner law.

marrow__PHYS_CH11_Q013.takeaway: Phantom-limb pain after amputation is the source-keyed example of cortical plasticity.
marrow__PHYS_CH11_Q013.displayText:
This patient has phantom-limb pain: pain perceived in the missing limb after amputation. Among the listed mechanisms, the source keys cortical plasticity. After loss of a body part, cortical representations can reorganize, and neighboring representations may extend into the cortical region formerly associated with the amputated part.

This reorganization is one recognized contributor to phantom-limb phenomena; the source's exam distinction is cortical plasticity rather than a change in the limb's peripheral sensory receptor.

rationales.a: Müller's law of specific nerve energies explains sensory modality by the pathway activated, not cortical remapping after amputation.
rationales.b: The labeled-line principle describes modality-specific pathways; the source asks for the post-amputation cortical reorganization associated with phantom pain.
rationales.d: Weber–Fechner relates sensation magnitude to stimulus intensity and does not explain phantom-limb pain.

marrow__PHYS_CH11_Q014.takeaway: Allodynia is pain caused by a normally innocuous sensory stimulus.
marrow__PHYS_CH11_Q014.displayText:
Allodynia is pain produced by a stimulus that normally does not provoke pain. Hyperalgesia is an exaggerated response to a noxious stimulus; for example, sunburned skin becomes unusually sensitive as local inflammatory mediators, including histamine and prostaglandins, sensitize pain endings.

Causalgia is a neuropathic pain syndrome, classically burning pain after nerve injury. Analgesia means reduced or absent pain. Therefore allodynia is the source-keyed term for painful perception of normal sensory input.

rationales.b: Hyperalgesia is an exaggerated response to a stimulus that is already noxious, rather than pain from an innocuous stimulus.
rationales.c: Analgesia is a reduction or absence of pain, the opposite of painful perception.
rationales.d: Causalgia is neuropathic pain associated with nerve injury, not the general definition of pain from normal sensory input.

marrow__PHYS_CH11_Q015.takeaway: Anandamide signaling is present in the periaqueductal gray pain-modulation system, making the source-keyed statement the best answer.
marrow__PHYS_CH11_Q015.displayText:
Anandamide (AEA) is an endogenous cannabinoid, alongside 2-arachidonoylglycerol (2-AG). These lipid mediators act at cannabinoid receptors CB1 and CB2. CB1 signaling is prominent in central pain circuits, while CB2 receptors are especially associated with immune and peripheral signaling; endocannabinoid action can produce antinociceptive effects in the appropriate circuit.

The source-keyed statement is that anandamide signaling occurs in the periaqueductal gray (PAG) and other pain-related regions. The wording “anandamide-containing neurons” is imprecise: primary experiments show stimulus-associated release of anandamide in the PAG, including after painful stimulation, rather than describing it as a conventional transmitter stored in a dedicated class of vesicle-filled neurons.

PAG endocannabinoid signaling and the descending opioid pathway are related pain-modulation systems but are not identical. PAG output recruits ventromedial medullary/raphe circuitry that can inhibit spinal nociceptive transmission, including through endogenous opioid signaling in downstream medullary pathways. The source's shorthand that the PAG itself releases endogenous opiates should not be read as a precise account of the full circuit; anandamide itself binds cannabinoid, not opioid, receptors.
emphasis: stimulus-associated release of anandamide in the PAG

rationales.a: Anandamide is produced endogenously; it is one of the endogenous cannabinoid ligands.
rationales.b: The source describes endocannabinoids as antinociceptive in this context, not as the nociceptive agent being contrasted here.
rationales.d: Anandamide acts through cannabinoid signaling, particularly CB1 in central pain pathways, rather than binding opioid receptors.

reconstruction.sourceProblem: The phrase “anandamide-containing neurons” may imply that this lipid mediator is stored like a conventional vesicular neurotransmitter. The source explanation also risks conflating PAG endocannabinoid modulation with the distinct descending opioid pathway.
reconstruction.reconstructedContent: The option remains the source-keyed best answer because anandamide is released and acts in PAG pain-modulatory circuits. The explanation describes stimulus-associated PAG release and distinguishes cannabinoid signaling from the opioid component of descending modulation.
evidenceBasis: Marrow ED8 Physiology Chapter 11, printed source page 213 (question/options), page 215 (answer key), and pages 221–222 (solution); source PDF SHA-256 recorded in the accompanying batch report.

marrow__PHYS_CH11_Q016.takeaway: Visceral pain is typically poorly localized and carried predominantly by small C fibers.
marrow__PHYS_CH11_Q016.displayText:
Visceral pain is commonly diffuse or poorly localized, unpleasant, and accompanied by autonomic symptoms such as nausea. It often arises from thoracic or abdominal organs and is transmitted mainly by small C fibers.

Visceral pain may be referred to a somatic region. A leading explanation is convergence of visceral and somatic afferents onto shared second-order neurons in the spinal dorsal horn; these neurons ascend to the thalamus and then the primary somatosensory cortex. The brain may attribute the signal to the more familiar somatic territory. Referred pain often follows shared segmental/dermatomal organization; the source gives the heart and arm as an example.

The source comparison below contrasts the fast Aδ component with the slow C-fiber component; it supports why visceral pain is associated with slow, poorly localized pain rather than fast pain. The source pairs Aδ fibers with glutamate and C fibers with substance P; these transmitter associations are retained here even though the table focuses on its four comparison rows.
emphasis: convergence of visceral and somatic afferents

displayTables.title: Source comparison of Aδ and C pain fibers

rationales.b: Visceral pain is not characteristically rapidly adapting; the source emphasizes persistent, poorly localized pain and autonomic features.
rationales.c: The source describes visceral pain as carried mainly by small C fibers, not B fibers.
rationales.d: Visceral pain is typically slow and diffuse, not the fast, sharply localized Aδ component.

marrow__PHYS_CH11_Q017.takeaway: Pulmonary alveoli are largely insensitive to pain, unlike the parietal pleura and stretched liver capsule.
marrow__PHYS_CH11_Q017.displayText:
Pulmonary alveoli and liver parenchyma are largely insensitive to pain. In contrast, the liver capsule is sensitive to direct trauma and stretch. Bile ducts, bronchi, arterial walls, and the parietal pleura are pain-sensitive.

Thus alveoli are the source-keyed pain-insensitive structure among these choices.
emphasis: liver capsule is sensitive to direct trauma and stretch

rationales.b: The liver capsule is sensitive to stretch and direct trauma, so it is not the pain-insensitive choice.
rationales.c: The parietal pleura is pain-sensitive, unlike the largely insensitive alveolar parenchyma.
rationales.d: Arterial walls contain pain-sensitive afferents and are not the source-keyed insensitive structure.

marrow__PHYS_CH11_Q018.takeaway: TENS can reduce pain by activating large-diameter Aβ touch afferents that engage inhibitory gating in the dorsal horn.
marrow__PHYS_CH11_Q018.displayText:
Transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation (TENS) can activate large-diameter, non-nociceptive Aβ touch-pressure afferents near the painful area. Their activity recruits inhibitory circuitry in the substantia gelatinosa of the dorsal horn, reducing transmission from nociceptive Aδ and C fibers: the gate-control model of pain modulation.

The source diagram traces nociceptive Aδ/C input toward ascending pathways and shows Aβ input acting through an inhibitory interneuron at the spinal gate. The same principle helps explain why rubbing or shaking an injured area, local vibration, and some counterirritants such as a mustard plaster may temporarily reduce pain. The source-keyed mechanism is gate theory, not referred pain, allodynia, or nonspecific analgesic action.
emphasis: inhibitory circuitry in the substantia gelatinosa

rationales.a: Referred pain is pain perceived at a site distant from its visceral or somatic source; it does not explain TENS analgesia.
rationales.c: Allodynia is pain caused by a normally innocuous stimulus, not the inhibitory mechanism by which TENS can relieve pain.
rationales.d: Analgesics may relieve pain pharmacologically, but the question asks for TENS's sensory-gating mechanism.

reconstruction.sourceProblem: The imported solution has OCR-corrupted Aδ/Aβ notation and describes an explanation figure whose labels must remain connected to the mechanism.
reconstruction.reconstructedContent: The scanned solution identifies TENS as gate-control analgesia at the dorsal-horn substantia gelatinosa: large Aβ touch-pressure input inhibits transmission from Aδ/C nociceptive afferents. The source also explicitly links touch, shaking, vibration, and counterirritants to this model.
